html:
A business analyst does not need to write Apex — but one who cannot specify what to automate and which tool to use hands ambiguity to developers and pays later. The declarative toolkit — validation rules, flows, approval processes, assignment rules — is the automation vocabulary every BA shares with the team, and this phase makes you literate enough to design it so delivery implements exactly what the stakeholder agreed to.

Learning Objectives

  • Design data-quality guardrails with validation rules and clearly worded error messages...
  • Explain what Flow Builder is and the difference between before-save, after-save, and screen flows...
  • Model a decision-and-sign-off gate using an approval process with queues and chains...
  • Route new records to the right owner with assignment rules and queues...
  • Recognize re-entry risk in declarative automation and specify a guard...
  • Select the right automation tool for a requirement using the repo's decision table...
  • Specify each of the six flows in the repo as a BA would write it down for delivery...
  • Read validation-rule and flow metadata in force-app and trace how the Apex services mirror them...

1. Why Declarative Automation Matters to a BA

Declarative automation means building behavior with point-and-click tools instead of hand-written code. For the BA it matters twice: you can see the rule running and show the stakeholder the guardrail they approved, and you can specify it as "if X then Y with message Z", exactly what a developer or admin needs.

The repo deliberately builds the same business rules twice — as Flow metadata and as an Apex service behind a trigger. Compare User_Story_Status_Transition with UserStoryService, or the backlog scoring flow with BacklogPrioritizationService; the two routes to the same behavior teach you where declarative tools express well and where they strain, which is the literacy for section 11.

2. Validation Rules: Guardrails, Not Gates

A validation rule protects data before bad data lands. It is a formula that, when it evaluates to true, blocks the save with an error message. Use validation for three job families: required checks (a field must be present), format checks (a field must look right), and range checks (a field must be bounded).

RuleFormula (simplified)Message
Value in rangeValue_Score__c > 100Score must be 1-100
Status needs criteriaISPICKVAL(Status__c,'Approved') && ISBLANK(Acceptance_Criteria__c)Add acceptance criteria first
Stories cappedStory_Points__c > 21Max 21 points per story

Word the message like a human, at the field: "Score must be 1-100" beats cryptic formula text — users read the message, not the formula. The repo ships validation rules on Business_Requirement__c in force-app/main/default/objects/Business_Requirement__c/; open one and read the formula and the error display text as a pair, because the pair is the deliverable.

Use validation rules sparingly, as guardrails at system boundaries, not gates on every interaction. A rule that fires a dozen times a day is a symptom of a bad experience or bad training, and "VIP users approve data errors internally" is not a guardrail, it is a hole.

3. Specifying Validation Rules as a BA

When the stakeholder asks for data protection, your specification should read like a sentence anyone can test:

  • The object and field(s) checked.
  • The condition under which the save FAILS (remember: the rule blocks when the formula is TRUE).
  • The exact error message, field-placement, and — if appropriate — the error tolerance (block vs. warn).
  • The exceptions (e.g., admin bypass) and who may override.
md
Requirement: REQ-VR-012
Object: User_Story__c
Check: Story_Points__c greater than 21
On condition TRUE -> block save with message: "Max 21 points per story."
Exceptions: none. Owner: BA, verified with team during backlog refinement.

A validation-rule requirement is testable in one click: try to save a violating record and read the error. Write several for BrightLogistics' lead routing — "Cannot set Status to Routed when Tier is blank" — and you have a quality model for the data your Phase 10 reports will trust.

4. Flows: The Automation Workbench

Flows are the platform's automations toolbox, and Flow Builder is its visual editor. A flow automates insert/update/approval logic in the same transaction or session — and record-triggered flows react to data changes, the same pattern the repo implements in its Apex services. The core notions:

  • A start — when the flow runs (record changed, button clicked, schedule, invoked by another flow).
  • Elements — decisions, updates, creates, get-records, loops, screens, subflows.
  • Triggers / start conditions — e.g., Record: User_Story__c Updated filtering to the status change that matters.
  • Resources — variables and formulas that hold state.

The BA reads flows as a sequence of decisions. Open force-app/main/default/flows/User_Story_Status_Transition.flow-meta.xml and you will see decision branches, an update element, and a guard condition — brain food for specifying your own flows.

5. Record-Triggered Flows: Before-Save vs. After-Save

Most business automation is record-triggered, so the before/after distinction is day-one literacy:

  • Before-save flows run in the same editing session, on the same record — cheap, ideal for setting or validating fields (populate a score, normalize text, block a value). They cannot touch other records.
  • After-save flows run after the record committed — ideal for creating or updating OTHER records (create a Task when a Case escalates, log a UAT defect, notify a queue via a platform event), including calling Apex services.

Choose by what the automation must do: "stamp the priority score on this record" is before-save; "create a follow-up Task and send the assignment to the dispatcher queue" is after-save. If you must create another record or call a service, after-save it is.

The repo's six flows use both patterns deliberately: Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring works on the record's own score, while Requirement_Approval_Routing coordinates routing across records. Read each flow and note its trigger kind — that reading habit is the fastest way to become flow-literate.

6. Screen Flows and Other Flow Types

Not every flow reacts to data. Screen flows guide a user through a wizard — collect a lead's details, show routing options, confirm dispatch — so they show up in feature definitions like "the dispatcher has a 3-step dispatch wizard".

Other types worth naming:

  • Scheduled flows run on a schedule — nightly re-scoring, expiry sweeps.
  • Autolaunched flows run in the background on demand or from another flow — reusable subroutines.
  • Platform event flows react to events — e.g., Requirement_Status_Changed__e picked up for notifications.

The BA's vocabulary stays the same: an input (what the flow needs), a process (the decisions), the output (the record changes or messages), and the error handling. For StudyBuddy Tutoring, a "send booking confirmation" screen flow takes tutor and session, checks capacity, writes the session, and confirms — a great first flow to doodle on paper before opening an editor.

7. The Six Flows in the Repository

The repo's six flows are your reference catalog — each is a named requirement pattern a BA would write:

FlowWhat it doesBA requirement it implements
Requirement_Approval_RoutingRoutes requirements through approval and publishes Requirement_Status_Changed__e"A requirement must be routed for approval before sign-off"
User_Story_Status_TransitionGoverns story status moves Backlog -> Refined -> In Progress -> Done"No story skips refinement; done follows a gate"
UAT_Defect_LoggingLogs a defect from a failed test case and notifies the story owner"A failing test case opens a defect for the owner"
Stakeholder_RSVP_TrackingRecords stakeholder RSVPs to discovery/workshop events and updates engagement"Workshop invitations tracked per RACI role"
Backlog_Prioritization_ScoringRecomputes Priority_Score__c from value weight minus effort"Re-rank the backlog whenever context changes"
Training_Question_ScoringActivates and scores question bank items in training"Activate only approved, correctly scored questions"

For each flow ask: what triggered it, which records does it touch, what gates does it enforce, and what would the error look like? That four-question habit turns a flow you see into a flow you can specify.

8. Guarding Against Re-Entry

Every after-save flow that updates a record can trigger itself again — a flow sets the status, the status change re-triggers the flow, and you get a loop or a duplicate action. This re-entry risk is the classic flow bug, and the BA's job is to specify the guard.

A common guard is a suppress flag: a checkbox like Flow_Skip_Trigger__c that the flow sets before its own update and checks in its start conditions, so the second pass exits immediately. The repo's Apex trigger framework uses the same pattern in its recursion guard (BATriggerHandlerService); find the guard by reading the start condition in User_Story_Status_Transition.

When you specify a flow that updates its own record, add one line to the requirement: "Flow must include a re-entry guard so a single user action produces exactly one execution." Testers can verify it by saving twice and counting side effects. Redundant saves, double notifications, and doubled Tasks are the visible symptoms of a missing guard.

9. Approval Processes: Decision Gates

An approval process adds an approve/reject step to a record's lifecycle — a decision gate, possibly in a chain. It consists of:

  • Entry criteria — which records enter the approval (e.g., Requirement_Type__c = 'High Impact').
  • Assignment — who approves, via a direct user, a role, or a queue.
  • Approval steps — sequential or parallel; a chain for escalating (analyst -> manager -> director).
  • Final actions — what happens after approval or rejection (sets Status, publishes an event, notifies the requester).

BrightLogistics uses the requirement approval process (force-app/main/default/approvalProcesses/Business_Requirement__c.Requirements_Approval.approvalProcess-meta.xml): a submitted requirement moves to Pending Approval, the designated reviewer approves or rejects, and on approval the status updates and Requirement_Status_Changed__e fires for downstream systems.

Specify an approval process as: who clicks submit, who approves, in what order, what each approval step may change, and what final actions run. The rule of thumb from the repo's decision table: "a manager must approve requirement status Approved" is approval-process territory because it is a decision gate with an owner, not a data transformation.

10. Assignment Rules and Queues

Assignment rules route new records to their first owner on create — initial routing, not reassignment. Queues hold unassigned work a team pulls from. In BrightLogistics, an assignment rule matches inbound leads on Source and Tier and drops them into the matching queue for dispatchers to claim.

The repo ships Lead and Case assignment rules in force-app/main/default/assignmentRules/. A BA names: rule order (first match wins), criteria per entry, target (user, owner, or queue), and queue membership. One such rule reads: "New leads with Source = Web and empty Tier go to the Web Lead Queue."

Assignment rules and queues are an after-save behavior but a distinctly "routing" one — later in a record's life, ownership changes belong to workflows, flows, or manual action, not assignment rules.

11. Choosing the Right Automation Tool

The decision table is the BA's shortcut to the right tool:

AutomationBest forDemo in repo
Validation ruleStop bad dataScore range, required criteria
FlowMulti-step automationRequirement routing, UAT defects
Approval processDecision gatesRequirement sign-off
Assignment ruleInitial routingLead intake, Case change requests
ApexComplex logic / APIsServices + triggers

The rule of thumb: start declarative, escalate to Apex only when logic needs loops, callouts, or scale — or when the declarative editor cannot express it. The repo's Apex services show the ceiling, the flows the floor. When a requirement cannot be a flow without forcing it, recommend Apex to the architect — and the BA's value is recognizing the boundary before the build.

Self-check: "a manager must approve requirement status Approved" — which tool? An approval process (queue + final approval actions), not a flow or validation rule, because it is a decision gate with sequential owner steps.

12. How a BA Specifies Declarative Automation

A complete automation requirement packs five sentences: trigger, condition, actions, error handling, and exceptions:

  1. Trigger — data change, schedule, button? On what object?
  2. Condition — the exact filter (start condition / entry criteria).
  3. Actions — what records change, what messages fire, what other records are created.
  4. Error handling — what the user sees when it fails, and the re-entry guard.
  5. Exceptions — who skips the rule and why.

That skeleton covers validation rules, flows, approvals, and assignment rules with one shape and maps 1:1 to what a developer or admin turns into metadata. Write the larger version of each of the six repo flows as a specification and you have a reusable portfolio. You are NOT specifying implementation detail: the BA names behavior and guardrails, and the team decides flow vs. Apex — unless the requirement explicitly asks for the escalation boundary.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 9.1 — Design a Validation Rule and Test the Block

Steps:

  1. Write a validation-rule requirement for User_Story__c: block a story marked "Must Have" with Story_Points__c blank.
  2. Implement it in the lab org (Setup, Validation Rules) with the message "Size the story before marking it Must Have."
  3. Try to save a violating record and capture the error; verify the "true = block" behavior both ways.

Expected result: a deployed rule whose message and trigger match the requirement exactly. What it proves: the formula-message pair is the whole contract and is testable in one click. (This is the seed pattern exercises 9.1 in Phase 15 ask you to scale.)

Exercise 9.2 — Trace a Record-Triggered Flow End to End

Steps:

  1. Open force-app/main/default/flows/User_Story_Status_Transition.flow-meta.xml and note its start object, start condition, decision branches, and update elements.
  2. Find the re-entry guard and explain in one sentence how it prevents a loop.
  3. In the lab, exercise the flow by moving a story Backlog -> Refined -> In Progress -> Done, and try an illegal backward jump.

Expected result: a one-page trace of the flow with the guard circled and a demonstrated blocked transition. What it proves: flows are decision sequences a BA can read, specify, and break-intentionally to test.

Exercise 9.3 — Specify an Approval Chain for BrightLogistics

Steps:

  1. Draft a requirement: inbound leads that go inactive for 5 days enter a "reactivation approval" — dispatcher submits, operations manager approves, auto-assignment then resumes.
  2. Fill in the five-sentence skeleton (trigger/condition/actions/errors/exceptions).
  3. Compare with Business_Requirement__c.Requirements_Approval in force-app/main/default/approvalProcesses/ and list the metadata counterparts of your sentences.

Expected result: a spec a developer could turn into metadata without asking a question. What it proves: approval specifications are decision gates with owners, steps, and final actions. (Approval + flow combos appear in exercise 9.3 of Phase 15.)

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Declarative automationBuilding platform behavior with point-and-click tools instead of code.
Validation ruleA formula that blocks a save when it evaluates to true, with an error message.
FlowA point-and-click automation; record-triggered, screen, scheduled, or invoked.
Before-save flowA flow updating fields on the same record within the same save transaction.
After-save flowA flow creating/updating other records or calling services after the commit.
Screen flowAn interactive wizard guiding a user step by step.
Re-entry guardA flag or start-condition that stops a flow from re-triggering itself.
Approval processA decision gate with approvers, steps or chains, and final actions.
Assignment ruleA rule routing newly created records to an owner or queue.
QueueA holding pool of unassigned records that a team claims.

Certification Checkpoints

  • Write a validation-rule requirement with the exact message users will see...
  • Explain before-save vs. after-save flows and pick the right one for a behavior...
  • Name and specify each of the repo's six flows as a requirement...
  • Detect re-entry risk in a flow and specify the guard...
  • Model an approval process with entry criteria, steps/chains, and final actions...
  • Route new records with assignment rules and queues using first-match logic...
  • Select between validation rule, flow, approval, assignment rule, or Apex using the repo's decision table...
  • Read flow and validation metadata in force-app and explain what the Apex services mirror...

Summary

You are now fluent in the declarative automation vocabulary: validation rules that guard data, flows that orchestrate behavior (including the six named flows in the repo), approval processes that gate decisions, and assignment rules plus queues that route work. You can specify any of them with the same five-sentence skeleton and explain the re-entry guard that keeps automation honest. That is the Automation & Flow section of your BA toolset — and the guardrails and rules you design here are exactly what the reports and dashboards of Phase 10 will watch over.
